title: The Churning of the Ocean
description: An illustrated map of the churning of the ocean of milk as tradition tells it, from Mount Mandara and the tortoise to the poison, the treasures, the nectar and the four Kumbh Mela towns, chapter by chapter.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the churning of the ocean of milk, set in the Bay of Bengal, with Mandar Hill, Kailasa, the Kumbh Mela towns and temples linked to the story
note: The ocean of milk (Kshirasagara) belongs to Puranic cosmology, not to any real sea; this map sets it in the Bay of Bengal only so the churning has a place on the page. Other places follow traditional associations, and where several claim one, the cards name them. The story follows the Bhagavata Purana and says where the Vishnu Purana and the Mahabharata differ. Neelkanth lies about 25 kilometres from Haridwar; here it is moved apart so each can be tapped. The map and the timeline are not to scale.

steps.title: A story told to Rama
steps.text: In the Ramayana, the epic behind Rama’s Journey, the sage Vishvamitra brings Rama and Lakshmana to the city of Vishala and tells them an old story from the first age (Krita Yuga): how the gods (devas) and the demons (asuras) churned the ocean for the nectar of immortality (amrita). The Mahabharata and the Puranas tell it too, with differences.
steps.today: Vaishali, Bihar, a great city in the Buddha’s time. The Ramayana says Vishala, a son of Ikshvaku, founded it.

steps.title: Durvasa’s garland
steps.text: In the Vishnu Purana, the short-tempered sage Durvasa gives Indra, king of the gods, a garland of flowers. Indra hangs it on his elephant, which flings it down and tramples it. Durvasa curses him: the three worlds will lose their good fortune (Shri). Plants wither, offerings stop and the gods grow weak.
steps.today: The Bhagavata Purana gives no curse: there, the gods are simply beaten in war.

steps.title: The gods defeated
steps.text: The demons, led by their king Bali, defeat the gods. Many gods fall and do not rise, while the demons’ teacher Shukracharya brings their own dead back to life. The beaten gods go to Brahma, the creator, who leads them to Vishnu to ask for help.
steps.today: Tradition sets these events in the heavens and on Mount Meru, which no map shows.

steps.title: Vishnu’s plan
steps.text: Vishnu tells them to make peace with the demons for now and churn the ocean of milk together, with Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent king Vasuki as the rope. Herbs are to be thrown into the sea. He warns them not to covet what rises first and not to lose their tempers.
steps.today: The ocean of milk (Kshirasagara) is part of Puranic cosmology. It is set in the Bay of Bengal here only for the map.

steps.title: A truce with Bali
steps.text: Indra goes to Bali and offers a truce. The demon king agrees: both sides will churn, and both will share the nectar. The gods keep Vishnu’s plan to themselves, for he has promised that only they will drink it.
steps.today: Bali returns in the story of Vamana, the dwarf avatar, and is remembered at Onam in Kerala.

steps.title: Uprooting Mandara
steps.text: Gods and demons tear Mount Mandara from the earth and try to carry it to the sea. It is too heavy. They drop it, and many are crushed beneath it. Vishnu arrives on his eagle Garuda, brings the crushed back to life and sets the mountain on Garuda’s back.
steps.today: Mandar Hill, Banka, Bihar, is the hill tradition names. A groove spiralling round it is said to be Vasuki’s mark. Puranic geography places Mandara beside Mount Meru.

steps.title: Garuda carries the mountain
steps.text: Garuda flies the mountain to the shore of the ocean of milk and lowers it into the water. Vasuki, king of the serpents, is promised a share of the nectar and agrees to be the rope. He coils himself round Mandara.
steps.today: Jains also hold Mandar Hill sacred to Vasupujya, the twelfth Tirthankara.

steps.title: Head or tail
steps.text: Vishnu and the gods take hold of the serpent’s head. The demons refuse to hold the tail, the lowly end, so the gods give way and take the tail themselves. Then the pulling begins. Fire and smoke from Vasuki’s breath scorch the demons, while clouds bring rain to the gods.
steps.today: Angkor Wat in Cambodia carves this tug of war along a gallery wall about 49 metres long, in the 12th century.

steps.title: The tortoise
steps.text: With nothing beneath it, the mountain sinks. Vishnu takes the form of a vast tortoise (Kurma), dives under the sea and holds Mandara up on his back. He also sits on the peak to hold it steady, and gives strength to gods, demons and serpent alike. The churning goes on.
steps.today: Kurma is the second of Vishnu’s ten avatars in the usual list.

steps.title: The tortoise’s temple
steps.text: Temples to Vishnu as the tortoise are rare. The best known is at Srikurmam, near the coast of Andhra Pradesh, where Kurma is worshipped as the main deity. Its walls carry inscriptions from the medieval kings of the region.
steps.today: Srikurmam, Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The poison
steps.text: In the Bhagavata, the first thing to rise is not nectar but a deadly poison (halahala). It spreads in every direction, burning everything it touches. Gods, demons and every creature flee, and Vishnu’s warning not to grab what comes first suddenly makes sense.
steps.today: The order of what rises differs between the Puranas and the Mahabharata.

steps.title: Shiva drinks the poison
steps.text: The gods go to Shiva on Mount Kailasa. Out of compassion, and with his wife Parvati’s consent, he gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. He holds it in his throat, which turns blue: he is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. The few drops that spill are taken up by snakes, scorpions and poisonous plants.
steps.today: Mount Kailash, in Tibet, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon.

steps.title: The blue throat
steps.text: Tradition places Shiva’s drinking of the poison, or his long rest afterwards, in the forested hills above Rishikesh, where the Neelkanth Mahadev temple stands. Pilgrims climb to it, especially in the monsoon month of Shravana, which is sacred to Shiva.
steps.today: Neelkanth Mahadev, near Rishikesh, Uttarakhand. On this map it is moved apart from Haridwar.

steps.title: Shiva at rest
steps.text: Another tradition says the poison made Shiva faint, and he lay down with his head in Parvati’s lap. At Surutapalli, the Pallikondeswarar temple shows him reclining so, a rare image of Shiva. South Indian tradition links Pradosham, a twice-monthly evening worship of Shiva, to this story.
steps.today: Surutapalli, Andhra Pradesh, near the Tamil Nadu border.

steps.title: The cow and the horse
steps.text: The churning resumes, and treasures rise. First comes the wish-granting cow (Kamadhenu, or Surabhi), which the sages take for the milk and butter of their fire rituals. Then a white horse, Uchchaihshravas, rises; the demon king Bali claims it.
steps.today: Popular retellings count fourteen treasures (ratnas), but the lists differ from text to text.

steps.title: The elephant and the jewel
steps.text: Next comes Airavata, a white elephant with four tusks, who becomes Indra’s mount. Then the jewel Kaustubha rises, and Vishnu takes it to wear on his chest.
steps.today: Airavata is carved as Indra’s mount on temples across India and Southeast Asia.

steps.title: The coral tree and the apsaras
steps.text: The coral tree (Parijata), whose flowers never fade, rises and goes to Indra’s heaven. After it come the apsaras, celestial dancers in fine clothes and jewels, who also make their home among the gods.
steps.today: Several flowering trees are called parijata in India, among them the night jasmine and the Indian coral tree.

steps.title: Lakshmi chooses
steps.text: Then Lakshmi, goddess of fortune (Shri), rises standing on a lotus. Everyone wants her. Sages bathe her and elephants pour water over her. She looks at each god and demon in turn and finds a flaw in all of them, then places her garland on Vishnu and makes his chest her home. Good fortune returns.
steps.today: Gajalakshmi, Lakshmi bathed by elephants, is carved on the gateways of Sanchi. She is worshipped at Diwali.

steps.title: The goddess of wine
steps.text: Varuni, goddess of wine, rises next, and with Vishnu’s consent the demons take her. In the Vishnu Purana and the Mahabharata, the moon also rises from the ocean during the churning; in many later tellings Shiva wears its crescent in his hair.
steps.today: In the Ramayana’s version, the gods (suras) are said to be named for accepting her, the demons (asuras) for refusing her.

steps.title: The physician
steps.text: Last rises Dhanvantari, a dark, young man in yellow, a form of Vishnu, holding a pot full of nectar. He is the physician of the gods, and tradition names him the founder of Ayurveda, India’s classical medicine.
steps.today: In 2016 India began marking National Ayurveda Day on Dhanteras, Dhanvantari’s festival before Diwali.

steps.title: The pot snatched
steps.text: The moment they see the pot, the demons snatch it and run. At once they quarrel among themselves over who should drink first. The gods, who did half the work, have nothing, and turn to Vishnu.
steps.today: Pots like this one (kalasha) appear at Indian weddings and temple rites as a sign of plenty.

steps.title: Mohini
steps.text: Vishnu appears among them as Mohini, an enchantress so beautiful that the demons stop fighting. They hand her the pot and ask her to share it out fairly. She seats gods and demons in two rows and serves the gods first, charming the demons into waiting their turn. Their turn never comes.
steps.today: Mohini returns in other Puranic stories, among them the tale of the demon Bhasmasura.

steps.title: Rahu at the table
steps.text: One demon, Rahu, disguises himself as a god and sits between the sun and the moon. He drinks, but they recognise him and cry out. Mohini’s discus cuts off his head before the nectar passes his throat. The head, made immortal, cannot die; Brahma makes it a planet.
steps.today: Later tradition names the headless body Ketu, a second shadow planet.

steps.title: Eclipses
steps.text: Rahu never forgives the sun and the moon. Tradition says that at every eclipse he chases and swallows one of them, but, having no body, he cannot keep it, and it comes out again. In Indian astrology, Rahu and Ketu are the two nodes of the moon’s orbit, where eclipses happen.
steps.today: Thirunageswaram, near Kumbakonam, Tamil Nadu, is the Rahu temple among the nine planet (Navagraha) temples of the Kaveri delta.

steps.title: War on the shore
steps.text: Cheated, the demons attack, but the gods have drunk the nectar. In the battle Indra strikes Bali down with his thunderbolt. The sage Narada persuades the gods to stop, and the demons carry their king home, where Shukracharya revives him.
steps.today: The Bhagavata tells this battle at length, naming many single combats.

steps.title: The tree goes to Dwaraka
steps.text: The coral tree stays in Indra’s garden until Krishna’s time. In The Life of Krishna, Krishna flies to Indra’s heaven on Garuda with his wife Satyabhama, uproots the tree for her and plants it at Dwaraka, beating the gods who try to stop him. After his death, says the Vishnu Purana, it returns to heaven.
steps.today: Dwaraka, Gujarat. Bhagavata Purana, book 10, and the Harivamsa.

steps.title: Four drops of nectar
steps.text: A later tradition, not in the Bhagavata or Vishnu Purana, says the pot (kumbha) was carried off, by Indra’s son Jayanta in some tellings, and chased for twelve days of the gods, twelve human years. Drops spilled at four places: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Ujjain and Nashik. They became the four sites of the Kumbh Mela.
steps.today: Each town holds a Kumbh about every twelve years, so one comes round about every three.

steps.title: Haridwar
steps.text: At Haridwar, where the Ganges leaves the mountains, pilgrims bathe at the Har ki Pauri ghat, which tradition calls the place a drop fell. The Kumbh is held when Jupiter is in Aquarius, the sign of the water pot (Kumbha), one reason given for the festival’s name.
steps.today: Haridwar, Uttarakhand. Some historians find the name Kumbh recorded for Haridwar earlier than for the other sites.

steps.title: Ujjain
steps.text: Ujjain’s Kumbh, on the Kshipra river, is called Simhastha because it falls when Jupiter is in Leo (Simha). The city is also home to Mahakaleshwar, one of the twelve great shrines of Shiva (jyotirlingas) Pilgrims bathe at Ramghat.
steps.today: Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Nashik
steps.text: Nashik’s Kumbh, also a Simhastha, is shared between the town, on the Godavari, and Trimbakeshwar, near the river’s source, where many ascetic orders bathe. Tradition also places part of Rama’s exile here, at Panchavati.
steps.today: Nashik and Trimbakeshwar, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Harsha at the confluence
steps.text: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang saw King Harsha hold a great assembly at Prayag, where the Ganges meets the Yamuna, giving away his treasury to monks, priests and the poor over many days, as he did every five years. Whether this was an early Kumbh Mela is debated.
steps.today: Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. The confluence is the Triveni Sangam; tradition adds a hidden third river, the Sarasvati.

steps.title: The Kumbh Mela today
steps.text: The Kumbh Mela is among the largest gatherings on Earth. Ascetic orders lead processions to bathe on the holiest days, and tens of millions follow. Official attendance counts are very large and disputed. In 2017 UNESCO listed the Kumbh Mela as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
steps.today: Prayagraj’s great Kumbh comes every twelve years; the last was in 2025.

items.name: Vishnu
items.role: The preserver, who plans the churning
items.text: One of the great gods of Hinduism, who keeps the world in order and takes new forms when it is in danger. In this story he is everywhere: the planner, Garuda’s rider, the tortoise beneath the mountain, Lakshmi’s choice, Dhanvantari with the nectar and Mohini at the table.

items.name: Indra
items.life: Vedic and Puranic tradition; no historical dates
items.text: The great warrior god of the Rigveda, wielder of the thunderbolt (vajra), who becomes in the Puranas the king of heaven, often proud and often in trouble. In the Vishnu Purana his careless treatment of Durvasa’s garland brings on the gods’ misfortune. He gains Airavata from the churning and strikes down Bali.

items.name: Bali
items.text: A demon king, grandson of the devoted Prahlada, generous and mighty. He agrees to the truce, claims the white horse and loses the war that follows. Later, in the story of Vamana, Vishnu as a dwarf asks him for three steps of land and takes the worlds back. Kerala remembers him at Onam.

items.name: Vasuki
items.role: King of the serpents, the churning rope
items.text: King of the serpents (nagas), often shown coiled round Shiva’s neck. He agrees to be the rope for a share of the nectar, and his fiery breath scorches the demons. A temple in Prayagraj’s Daraganj is dedicated to him, and Nag Panchami, the serpents’ festival, honours nagas like him.

items.name: Shiva
items.text: One of the great gods of Hinduism, the ascetic of Mount Kailasa. When the poison threatens every creature, he drinks it and holds it in his throat, which turns blue, earning the name Nilakantha. Many tellings give him the crescent moon from the churning, worn in his hair.

items.name: Lakshmi
items.text: Goddess of wealth, beauty and good fortune, also called Shri. In this story she rises from the ocean on a lotus and chooses Vishnu as her husband, ending the gods’ misfortune. She is worshipped at Diwali, and often shown bathed by two elephants (Gajalakshmi).

items.name: Dhanvantari
items.text: A form of Vishnu who rises from the ocean carrying the pot of nectar. He is the physician of the gods and tradition’s founder of Ayurveda. Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, is his festival, and India first marked National Ayurveda Day on it in 2016.

items.name: Rahu
items.role: The demon who tastes the nectar
items.text: A demon who slips in among the gods and drinks the nectar before he is caught. Beheaded, his immortal head becomes a planet and chases the sun and moon at eclipses. Later tradition calls the body Ketu. Both are among the nine planets (Navagraha) worshipped in Indian astrology.

items.name: Shukracharya
items.text: The demons’ teacher and priest, a son of the sage Bhrigu, who knows the secret of bringing the dead back to life (sanjivani). His power gives the demons the upper hand at the start, and he revives Bali after the war. The planet Venus bears his name, Shukra.

items.name: Durvasa
items.role: The sage whose curse starts it all
items.text: A sage famous for his temper, who appears across the epics and Puranas cursing those who slight him and blessing those who serve him well. In the Vishnu Purana, his curse on Indra drains the world of good fortune and sets the churning in motion.
